text: Salvador Domingo Felipe Jacinto Dalí i Domènech, Marquess of Dalí de Púbol (11 May 1904 – 23 January 1989), known as Salvador Dalí, was a Spanish surrealist artist celebrated for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre imagery. Born on 11 May 1904 at 8:45 am on the first floor of Carrer Monturiol, 20 in Figueres, Catalonia, Spain, near the French border, Dalí's older brother, also named Salvador (born 12 October 1901), had died of gastroenteritis on 1 August 1903. His father, Salvador Luca Rafael Aniceto Dalí Cusí (1872–1950), was a middle-class lawyer and notary, an anti-clerical atheist and Catalan federalist, whose strict discipline was softened by his wife, Felipa Domènech Ferrés (1874–1921), who encouraged Dalí’s artistic development. In 1912, the family moved to the top floor of Carrer Monturiol 24 (now 10). Dalí later attributed his love for luxury, gilded things, and oriental clothing to an "Arab lineage," claiming his ancestors were descendants of the Moors. He was haunted by his dead brother throughout his life, describing them as "like two drops of water, but with different reflections," and later referred to his brother as "probably the first version of myself but conceived too much in the absolute." Images of his brother reappeared in works such as Portrait of My Dead Brother (1963). Dalí also had a sister, Anna Maria, who was three years younger, and he painted her 12 times between 1923 and 1926. Childhood friends included future FC Barcelona footballers Emili Sagi-Barba and Josep Samitier, with whom they played football during holidays in Cadaqués. Dalí attended the Municipal Drawing School in Figueres in 1916 and discovered modern painting during a summer trip to Cadaqués with the family of Ramon Pichot, a local artist who traveled to Paris. In 1918, he held his first public exhibition at the Municipal Theatre in Figueres, a venue he returned to decades later. In 1921, the Pichot family introduced him to Futurism, and his uncle Anselm Domènech, who owned a bookshop in Barcelona, supplied him with books on Cubism and contemporary art. On 6 February 1921, Dalí’s mother died of uterine cancer; at 16, he later described the loss as the greatest blow in his life, saying he worshipped her and could not accept her death. After her death, his father married her sister, which Dalí did not resent due to his deep respect for his aunt. In 1922, Dalí moved to the Residencia de Estudiantes in Madrid and studied at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando. Standing 1.72 metres tall, he was known as an eccentric and dandy with long hair, sideburns, a coat, stockings, and knee-breeches in the style of late 19th-century English aesthetes. At the Residencia, he became close to Pepín Bello, Luis Buñuel, Federico García Lorca, and others in the Madrid avant-garde group Ultra; his friendship with Lorca was emotionally intense, though Dalí rejected the poet’s sexual advances, and the relationship remained significant until Lorca’s death in 1936 during the Spanish Civil War. In 1922, he began a lifelong relationship with the Prado Museum, visiting every Sunday to study the masters, which he described as the start of a "monk-like period" devoted to solitary work. His Cubist paintings, such as Cabaret Scene (1922) and Night-Walking Dreams (1922), drew attention from peers, as there were no Cubist artists in Madrid at the time. In May 1925, he exhibited eleven works at the Sociedad Ibérica de Artistas in Madrid, seven in Cubist style and four in realism, earning praise from critics. His first solo exhibition at Galeries Dalmau in Barcelona, from 14 to 27 November 1925, included twenty-two works and was a critical and commercial success. In April 1926, Dalí traveled to Paris, where he met Pablo Picasso, whom he revered, and was influenced by Yves Tanguy, later claiming to have "pinched everything from your uncle Yves." He left the Royal Academy in 1926, shortly before his final exams, and demonstrated mastery through his realistic painting The Basket of Bread (1926). In December 1926 to January 1927, he exhibited again at Galeries Dalmau with the support of critic Sebastià Gasch, featuring twenty-three paintings and seven drawings, with the Cubist works separated from the objective ones; the critical response was generally positive, with Composition with Three Figures (Neo-Cubist Academy) receiving special attention. From 1927, Dalí’s work became increasingly influenced by Surrealism. Works such as Honey is Sweeter than Blood (1927) and Gadget and Hand (1927), shown at the Barcelona Autumn Salon in October 1927, were described by Dalí as "equidistant between Cubism and Surrealism" and featured dreamlike images, precise draftsmanship, idiosyncratic iconography (like rotting donkeys and dismembered bodies), and landscapes evocative of Catalonia. These works caused bemusement among the public and debate among critics about whether he had become a Surrealist. Influenced by Freud and Lautréamont, Dalí introduced suggestive sexual imagery into his work; Dialogue on the Beach (Unsatisfied Desires) (1928) was rejected by the Barcelona Autumn Salon for being too provocative, sparking a scandal widely covered in the press and prompting a Madrid illustrated weekly to publish an interview with Dalí. Throughout the 1920s, Dalí was influenced by a range of styles, from classical masters like Raphael, Bronzino, Francisco de Zurbarán, Vermeer, and Velázquez to avant-garde movements, resulting in a mixture of praise and puzzled debate from critics due to the blend of traditional and modern techniques. In the mid-1920s, he grew a neatly trimmed mustache, later cultivating a more flamboyant one in the style of Diego Velázquez, which became a well-known Dalí icon. In 1929, Dalí collaborated with Luis Buñuel on the short film Un Chien Andalou (An Andalusian Dog), contributing to the script, though contemporary accounts do not substantiate a significant role in filming. That same year, he met his lifelong muse and future wife Gala, born Elena Ivanovna Diakonova, a Russian immigrant ten years his senior who was then married to poet Paul Éluard. In works such as The First Days of Spring, The Great Masturbator, and The Lugubrious Game, Dalí explored themes of sexual anxiety and unconscious desires. His first Paris exhibition at the Goemans Gallery in November 1929 featured eleven works, with André Breton describing the work as "the most hallucinatory that has been produced up to now"; the exhibition was commercially successful but critically divided. In 1929, Dalí officially joined the Surrealist group in Montparnasse, Paris, and the Surrealists recognized his paranoiac-critical method of accessing the subconscious. His relationship with his father deteriorated due to his romance with Gala and his association with Surrealism; the final incident occurred when his father read in a Barcelona newspaper that Dalí had exhibited a drawing of the Sacred Heart of Jesus with the inscription "Sometimes, I spit for fun on my mother's portrait," leading to a public demand for recantation. Dalí refused, possibly fearing expulsion from the Surrealist group, and was violently thrown out of his home on 28 December 1929, with his father declaring he would be disinherited and barred from Cadaqués. The following summer, Dalí and Gala rented a small fisherman’s cabin in Port Lligat, which he later bought and expanded into a beloved seaside villa. His father eventually accepted his son’s companion. In 1931, Dalí painted The Persistence of Memory, featuring soft, melting pocket watches, interpreted as a rejection of rigid time, supported by expansive landscapes and watches being devoured by ants. In June 1931 and May–June 1932, he held two exhibitions at the Pierre Colle Gallery in Paris, with the first including sixteen paintings, of which The Persistence of Memory drew the most attention. The exhibitions featured images of Gala and Surrealist objects such as Hypnagogic Clock and Clock Based on the Decomposition of Bodies. His largest exhibition at Pierre Colle in June 1933 included twenty-two paintings, ten drawings, and two objects, with one critic noting his precise draftsmanship and calling him a "paranoiac of geometrical temperament." His first New York exhibition at Julien Levy’s gallery in November–December 1933 featured twenty-six works and was a commercial and critical success, with The New Yorker praising the precision and lack of sentimentality, calling them "frozen nightmares." Dalí and Gala were civilly married on 30 January 1934 in Paris and later remarried in a church ceremony on 8 August 1958 at Sant Martí Vell. Gala managed Dalí’s business affairs, supporting their extravagant lifestyle while avoiding insolvency, and despite her own extra-marital affairs, she tolerated Dalí’s relationships with younger muses, remaining his primary partner. Dalí continued to paint Gala as they aged, producing sympathetic and adoring images. Their long, tense, complex, and ambiguous relationship, lasting over 50 years, became the subject of the opera Jo, Dalí (I, Dalí) by Catalan composer Xavier Benguerel. Dalí’s first U.S. visit in November 1934 attracted widespread press coverage; his second New York exhibition at Julien Levy in November–December 1934 was again a commercial and critical success. He delivered three lectures on Surrealism at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and other venues, stating for the first time that "[t]he only difference between me and a madman is that I am not mad." The heiress Caresse Crosby organized a farewell fancy dress ball on 18 January 1935, where Dalí wore a glass case on his chest containing a brassiere and Gala dressed as a woman giving birth through her head; a Paris newspaper claimed the Dalís dressed as the Lindbergh baby and his kidnapper, a claim Dalí denied. While most Surrealists aligned with leftist politics, Dalí maintained an ambiguous stance on politics and art. André Breton accused Dalí of defending the "new" and "irrational" in "the Hitler phenomenon," but Dalí rejected the claim, stating, "I am Hitlerian neither in fact nor intention," and insisted that Surrealism could exist in an apolitical context, refusing to explicitly denounce fascism.
